passages.where: Jesus says that if you are at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift, go and be reconciled, and then come back. The site's note puts it simply: worship waits for reconciliation. The plain note adds that this does not mean a person who has been harmed must go back to someone dangerous, because making peace takes two, and sometimes the safest and most honest step is distance and help from others.

More than twenty years after selling Joseph, his brothers stand accused in Egypt and say to one another that they saw his anguish when he pleaded with them and would not listen. The site's note says this is the first time the reader learns that Joseph begged them from the pit; the story kept silent about it until their consciences spoke. Reconciliation in this family begins long before the embrace, with guilt finally named.

Met by Esau's embrace instead of his army, Jacob presses his gift on his brother and tells him that seeing his face is like seeing the face of God, since he has received him favorably. The site's note says the face Jacob now sees has turned toward him in welcome, the second face he did not expect to survive. The note on the chapter also says the brothers then went separate ways, and readers can hold both a real reconciliation and a man still learning to speak plainly.

The law tells a person who has wronged a neighbor to confess the sin, make full restitution, add a fifth, and give it to the one wronged. The site's note lists this among the laws that protect the camp where God dwells. Repair in Scripture is concrete: it names the wrong and puts back more than was taken.

When Jesus comes to his house, Zacchaeus stands up and promises half his goods to the poor and fourfold repayment to anyone he has cheated. The site's note says he answers the crowd's grumbling with deeds rather than argument, and that Jesus' welcome came before he said a word about money. Grace comes first; then repentance reaches the purse and the people wronged.

Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon as a beloved brother and writes that if he owes anything, Philemon should charge it to Paul's account. The site's plain note says Paul did not leave the matter to chance: he wrote in front of the whole church, paid what was owed, and said he was coming to see. It also says plainly that this letter must never be used to send anyone back to a place where they are mistreated.

Paul pleads with Euodia and Syntyche, two women who had labored beside him for the gospel, to agree in the Lord, and asks a trusted companion in the church to help them. The site's note calls them two leaders. Paul names the conflict, honors both women, and brings in a third person to help, rather than taking sides from a distance.

Paul says that all this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, not counting people's trespasses against them. The site's note sets it in a chapter about the new creation that everyone in Christ already is. Every human reconciliation Christians attempt is an echo of one God has already made, at his own cost.

Paul says Christ himself is our peace, who made Jew and Gentile one and tore down the dividing wall of hostility, reconciling both to God in one body through the cross. The site's notes say the cross that killed Christ also killed the hostility, and that the wall he broke down was hostility, not a people. The peace between people rests on the peace with God.

misread.taken: Jesus' steps for going to a brother who has sinned against you are used to require someone who was harmed, even abused, to meet privately with the person who hurt them, or to silence anyone who raises a concern by asking whether they went to him first.
misread.says: The site's plain note says this passage has been badly misused, and that it must be faced. Matthew 18 is not a rule that makes a harmed person meet the one who harmed them, and nothing in it asks a child, or anyone who is afraid, to go alone to the person who hurt them. The steps are for wrongs between believers who stand on roughly equal ground; they do not fit a case where one person has power over another. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, and nothing in these verses puts a church meeting in their place.

whole: If the person you are thinking of has harmed you or your children, reconciliation is not your first task; safety is, and no passage in the Bible asks you to go back into danger. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. For many people, though, the broken relationship is not dangerous, only painful: the friend who stopped calling after an argument, the brother who did not come to the wedding, the church split that ended a friendship, the colleague you avoid in the hallway, the apology you have rehearsed for years and never made. Some want to make peace and do not know where to begin. Some have tried and been rebuffed. Some know they were mostly in the wrong and dread the conversation that would admit it.

Repair is hard for reasons Scripture knows well. Joseph's brothers carried their guilt for more than twenty years before they could say aloud what they had seen in the pit. Jacob prepared gifts and bowed seven times because he did not know what his brother's face would hold. Pride makes it hard to name our own part; fear makes it hard to hear the other person's account of us; unequal power can make any meeting unsafe; and each side often remembers a different story, both of them partly true. Most of us would rather wait for the other person to move first. That waiting has ended more friendships than any single quarrel.

So the Bible's wisdom is to tell the difference between forgiveness and reconciliation, and then to do the part that is yours. Forgiveness can be given by one person, and it lets go of revenge; reconciliation takes two, and it is built on truth. If you were in the wrong, go first, as Jesus told the worshiper at the altar to do; confess your part specifically and without excuses, and make it right where you can, as the law and Zacchaeus did. Do not make your apology wait on theirs. If you were wronged, you may name the wrong, ask for what you need, and take time before trust returns. A wise third person can help, as Paul asked a companion to help two women in Philippi. Some reconciliations end in close friendship, and some, like Jacob and Esau's, end in peace kept at a respectful distance. Both are real. And no one may use any of this to press a person who is afraid to meet the one who harmed them.

The hope Scripture gives is that reconciliation is God's own work before it is ours. While we were his enemies he reconciled us to himself through the death of his Son, not counting our trespasses against us, and he has given the message of reconciliation to his people. On the cross Christ tore down the wall of hostility, and he is the peace that people on both sides of a quarrel can share. In the psalm, loving devotion and faithfulness meet and righteousness and peace kiss. Not every relationship will be mended in this life. But in Christ, peace that is true and peace that is just are no longer enemies.
sit: Is there someone with something against you whom you have been waiting to move first, and what would it look like for you to go, honestly and safely, this week?

prayer.lead: A prayer that listens for God to speak peace, where loving devotion and faithfulness meet and righteousness and peace kiss.
